source: Murphy (2026) Agentic Forecasting with Structured Linguistic Beliefs (BLF), arXiv 2604.18576 v5
finding: Paired comparison on shared ForecastBench questions: BLF (Gemini 3.1 Pro, ReAct with belief state, 5 trials averaged) beats the leaderboard agents Cassi, Grok 4.20 and Foresight-32B. All of them get the market price for market questions. This is the first source that puts Cassi and Grok 4.20 on common questions with paired tests.
numbers: 400 question-date instances (355 questions, 791 resolution events), tranches 2025-10-26 and 2025-11-09. Overall Brier Index (higher better): BLF 73.3, Cassi 70.8 (paired diff -2.4, significant), Grok 4.20 70.5 (-1.4, ns, tranche A only), Foresight 69.3 (-5.6). Market: BLF 83.8, Cassi 82.0 (-1.7 ns). Data: BLF 62.7, Cassi 59.6 (-3.1). Leaderboard ABI: Cassi (ensemble+crowd-adj) 67.9, Grok 67.8, Foresight 67.2.
limits: One paper, one author, frozen April 2026 snapshot; Grok and Foresight each cover only one tranche; BLF built by the paper's author. Question difficulty explains 62% of score variance, so unpaired leaderboard gaps are weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Shows that the top entries differ by only 1-3 Brier Index points once paired; the ranking of Cassi and Grok is not a clear sign that one trick (search, 8 runs, crowd adjustment) is worth more than another.

source: Murphy (2026) BLF Table 2: comparison to the LLM-free crowd+empirical-prior baseline
finding: Just returning the market price (market questions) plus the base rate (dataset questions) already scores about as well as the top agents. Only BLF is significantly above it overall. Cassi and Grok trend positive but are not significant. So the crowd-adjustment step of Cassi cannot be credited with a large real gain on top of the price.
numbers: Crowd+prior baseline Brier Index: market 81.5, data 58.3, overall 69.9. Paired gain over baseline, overall: BLF +3.4 (significant), Cassi +1.0 (ns), Grok +0.1 to +1.0 (ns), Foresight -1.5 (ns). Market only: Cassi +0.6 (ns), BLF +2.3 (ns). Data only: BLF +4.5 (significant).
limits: Table text extracted from PDF with some row jumbling; the Cassi and Grok rows were matched by arithmetic against Table 1. Unadjusted bootstrap tests, 5000 resamples.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the near-0.01 crowd-adjustment gain reported by FRI is a gain over Cassi's own un-adjusted ensemble, not over the market price. Against the price, Cassi's market gain is +0.6 Brier Index points (about 0.006 Brier) and not significant. A plain price anchor is a very strong baseline to beat.

source: Murphy (2026) BLF: multi-trial averaging, logit vs arithmetic, LLM aggregation of traces
finding: Averaging K trials of the same agent improves Brier Index as K grows; logit averaging gives only a small extra boost; leave-one-out shrinkage toward 0.5 picks no shrinkage (q=1). The AIA-style LLM aggregator that reads all reasoning traces did worse than a plain mean on ForecastBench. Arithmetic-mean gain is guaranteed in expectation by Jensen's inequality, but only against the average single trial, not the best one.
numbers: K=5 default. Fig 2a: 400 FB questions, no crowd anchor, Brier Index axis spans about 68.5 to 69.5 across K=1..5 (read from figure; exact values not printed). Logit averaging degrades more gracefully when one trial fails: with p=0.95 and one dead trial in five, arithmetic mean loses about 9 points of probability, logit mean about 4.
limits: Exact per-K numbers are only in a figure. Preliminary AIA-aggregator comparison is stated as 'not reported here'.
agent_relevance: Supports S3 'average K independent runs by plain mean or logit mean'; argues against an LLM that re-reads all traces (gap 4/8).

source: Murphy (2026) BLF Table 3: belief-state ablation and cross-trial spread of reasoning models
finding: Adding a structured belief state (probability plus evidence summary carried between search steps) helped two Gemini backbones but not GPT-5.4. Cross-trial standard deviation on market questions was large for a reasoning model without the belief state and fell sharply with it.
numbers: Overall gain from belief state (Brier Index): Gemini-3.1-Pro +3.00 [1.95, 4.25]; Gemini-3-Flash +1.99 [1.12, 3.02]; GPT-5.4 -0.42 [-0.86, 0.002]. Market-question cross-trial SD: Pro 0.094 to 0.030, Flash 0.105 to 0.032, GPT slightly up. N=400 (399 for Flash).
limits: Authors do not know why; one earlier Kimi-K2.5 result dropped because of submission failures, not forecast quality.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a frontier reasoning model still has run-to-run SD near 0.09-0.10 on market questions, so averaging is not obsolete for reasoning models. A structured carried-forward state reduces spread, which shrinks the room that averaging has to fill.

source: Murphy (2026) BLF Section B: four-layer leakage defense and audit
finding: A runtime LLM classifier that drops post-cutoff search results catches nearly all leaks but throws away many clean results too. A second LLM audit finds a small residual leak rate among kept results.
numbers: n=2,272 search results, tranche A: filter recall 93.8% (320 of 341 leaks caught); 577 clean results dropped (29.9% false positive rate); 1,377 results kept, 21 leaks (1.5% residual). At least one flagged result for 14 of 76 web-search questions (18.4%), 7.0% of all 200 tranche-A questions.
limits: Second-LLM verdicts, not human ground truth; exposure rate does not measure effect on forecasts.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: filtering costs about 30% of genuine pages under this setup (the earlier 39% figure is another study); a filter-then-audit pipeline gives 1.5% residual leaks. Leak removal and poison removal are different jobs; this audit only covers date leaks.

source: Murphy (2026) BLF Section C.7: crowd and empirical priors
finding: For market questions the freeze value (market price or Metaculus community prediction) is injected as an anchor and adds a lot. Just predicting the price scores Brier Index about 81.5. For dataset questions the base-rate prior scores 58.3 and the full BLF 62.7.
numbers: Market price alone BI 81.5; empirical-prior alone on dataset questions 58.3; BLF 62.7. Base rates are very low in the sample: Polymarket 11%, Manifold 18%, Metaculus 15%, RFI 0%.
limits: Low base rates make price and prior anchoring look strong; transfer to balanced question sets is untested.
agent_relevance: Base-rate-first (gap 6): giving the agent a reference-class prior before search is standard in this best frontier system, and it is a strong baseline by itself.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: Technical Report, arXiv 2511.07678, Section 7.1
finding: Averaging independent runs beats a single random run. Mean, trimmed mean and median are interchangeable. Most of the gain comes in the first 5 runs, with a small extra gain up to 15. Single-run performance is highly variable even over 1,610 questions.
numbers: FB-7-21 (1,610 questions): single forecast Brier 0.1182; mean of 10 0.1140; trimmed mean 0.1142; median 0.1138. MarketLiquid: sharp drop from 1 to 5 runs, modest gain 5 to 15 (bootstrap from 50 forecasts per question; values in a figure). Authors use 10 runs.
quote: Brier score for the average forecast and outcome is a strict improvement on the Brier score averaged over possible forecasts
limits: Comparison is at equal question, not equal tokens. Vendor-style technical report, no peer review.
agent_relevance: Independent confirmation of Halawi's small ensemble gain (about 0.004 here vs 0.003 there); settles that the choice of mean/median/trimmed does not matter. Does not answer gap 1 (equal tokens).

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster Section 7.2: supervisor agents for aggregation
finding: An LLM that reads the 10 forecasts and only rewrites them (Halawi style) did worse than the plain mean. An agentic supervisor that finds disagreements, searches to resolve them, and only replaces the mean when it is highly confident did best.
numbers: FB-7-21 Brier: agentic supervisor 0.1125; non-agentic supervisor 0.1168; best-of-k 0.1191; none (single) 0.1199. The paper's text also says a plain mean is substantially better than the non-agentic LLM aggregation because LLMs overweight outlier opinions.
limits: Different table baselines (None 0.1199 vs single 0.1182 in Table 9) show subset or sampling differences. Gain of the agentic supervisor over mean 0.1140 is about 0.0015, small and untested for significance.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 and 4: selecting or rewriting members by LLM judgement is a risk; the one variant that worked adds new search and falls back to the mean unless confidence is high.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster Section 5.1: search quality and market-price access (Tables 3 and 4)
finding: Search quality matters: the weakest non-agentic search equals no search, agentic search with a good provider helps. Giving the forecaster the market price closes about 42% of the gap between no-search and agentic-search, and the price alone beats the best Karger 2024 LLM forecaster that was given it.
numbers: ForecastBench Brier: none 0.1230; Search-B non-agentic 0.12168; Search-B agentic 0.11824; Search-A non-agentic 0.11738; Search-A agentic 0.1140. Market-question subset: no search 0.116; no search plus price 0.103; price alone 0.096; agentic search 0.085; agentic search plus price 0.075.
limits: Authors anonymise search providers. Their foreknowledge-bias filtering is applied, but the benchmark is theirs.
agent_relevance: Gap 2/3: with a leak-mitigated pipeline, good retrieval is worth about 0.009 Brier overall and about 0.03 on market questions without the price; the price itself is worth about 0.010-0.013. This is the largest-effect crowd adjustment with a clean ablation, and it is about the same size as the Cassi claim.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster Section 7.3: Platt scaling and log-odds extremization
finding: LLM forecasts are hedged toward the middle. Scaling log-odds away from 0.5 (extremizing) or Platt scaling lowers Brier even after averaging. Largest drops occur for forecasts in 0.2-0.4 and 0.6-0.8.
numbers: FB-7-21 Brier: none 0.1140; log-odds extremization (fixed d=3) 0.1085; Platt scaling fixed parameter 0.1076; Platt ID-trained 0.1071; Platt OOD-trained 0.1104; isotonic and OLS worse. Platt on arithmetic mean was best.
limits: Opposite direction to Corroboration Illusion, where retrieval pushes means up (optimism bias). The two corrections address different biases: hedging vs inflation.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: ensemble then extremize is a tested fix for under-confidence; it does not fix the upward shift from retrieved news, which needs a base-rate step or per-document aggregation (d16). BLF found Platt gave +0.7 to +1.5 Brier Index.

source: Aitchison, Jeen, Shevlane, Day (2026) Diversity is the Strength of the AI Crowd, arXiv 2606.29661 (ICML 2026 workshop)
finding: At a fixed number of samples, the best ensemble never puts all samples on the single strongest model. Frontier models give highly correlated forecasts, so a second draw from the same model adds little. Grok 4 is the least replaceable member even though third in solo score because it is least correlated with the others.
numbers: Metaculus AI Benchmark Q2 2025, N=113 binary questions, 5 models (Gemini 3 Pro, GPT-5, Grok 4, Kimi K2.5, fine-tuned gpt-oss-120b), up to 3 runs per model, budget B=5 brute-forced (101 valid allocations). Optimal B=5 team: FT 2, Gemini 1, GPT-5 1, Grok 1. Replaceability: Grok about 1.7 baseline points, FT about 0.6, GPT-5 and Gemini under 0.1 each. Three-model mix GPT-5 + Gemini only gains at most about 0.6 points over better single; moving toward FT picks up about 2.7 points.
limits: Small N (113), one tournament, no bootstrap intervals (authors say magnitudes are indicative, ranking is the robust result); includes a fine-tuned model (training, not scaffolding); same scaffold for all.
agent_relevance: Best direct answer to gap 4 and part of gap 1: at equal calls, mix models (or at least decorrelated personas) rather than copies. Also explains why a Grok-containing system can rank high (gap 7).

source: Peng, Luo, Chen, Tang (2026) Two Heads Are Better Than One: Aggregating Weaker LLMs for Better Forecasts, arXiv 2609.33257
finding: On ForecastBench subquestions, a learned linear pool of two weaker models matches or beats the strongest single model in 11 of 16 groups and comes within 5% of its Brier in all 16. Adding more members past three does not help consistently.
numbers: 70 LLM forecasters, 16 comparison groups, each over 1,000 shared subquestions, 1,121 weaker pairs. Learned linear pooling: success groups 11/16 (2 models), 12/16 (3), 11/16 (4 and 5). Learned log-odds pooling: 8/16 (2), 11/16 (3), 11/16 (4, 5). Group G13 best pool 0.848 for sizes 2 to 5.
limits: Weights are learned on separate training data; this needs history, which a single agent does not have. Score scale in group G13 (0.848) is not plain Brier. Lower ECE need not mean lower Brier.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: the flattening point for different-model pools is about 3 members. Fixed-weight equal averaging is the safe choice for an agent without training data.

source: LLM-SoccerArena (2026) Benchmarking LLMs on Real-World Predictions in Sports, arXiv 2607.24573
finding: Seven LLMs forecasting World Cup 2026 matches gave almost the same probabilities, so an equal-weight ensemble was no better than the average member in a way that survives multiple-testing correction.
numbers: Mean pairwise correlation between model home/draw/away probabilities 0.943. Equal-weight ensemble improves on the average member by only 0.0047 Brier; none of the seven ensemble-vs-member contrasts significant after Holm correction.
limits: Sports match outcomes with 3-way probabilities, not binary forecasting questions; read from two-column PDF text, so some detail may be missed; small sample.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 negative boundary: model diversity only pays when members disagree. When models are 0.94 correlated, ensembling over them is near worthless.

source: Liu et al. (2026) CHAIN: Calibrated LLM Forecasting via Causal-Temporal Hypergraph Inference, arXiv 2609.36689, Appendix L
finding: A compute-controlled test: one forecast, the average of five independent forecasts, and a structured 5-call method on the same 8 datasets with DeepSeek-V3. Five-sample averaging gives only a small gain; the structured method with a similar number of calls gives much more.
numbers: Macro average over 8 datasets. Direct (1 call, 550 tokens): ECE 15.21, Brier 23.47, Acc 60.25. Five-sample average (about 2,751 tokens): ECE 14.91, Brier 23.07, Acc 60.84. CHAIN (5.0 calls, about 13,371 tokens): ECE 8.14, Brier 19.89, Acc 70.02. Averaging gain 0.40 Brier points (0.004).
limits: Not the same setting as search-forecasting: these are time-series/event datasets with a weak base model (DeepSeek-V3, plain direct prompt); CHAIN uses about 5x the tokens of the 5-average, so tokens are not equal; no variance or CIs; the method is the authors' own.
agent_relevance: Closest thing to gap 1: spending the same number of calls on structure instead of repeats can beat repeats. Equal TOKENS were not matched (CHAIN used 4.9x the tokens of the 5-average), so the question stays open.

source: FutureSearch (2026-05-01) Run agents twice for fun and profit (blog)
finding: Two runs of the same top agent tie on average score but differ on single questions; averaging four runs from different models beat one run. The post argues repeating is cheaper than improving the agent.
numbers: BTF-2, 1,367 questions: single Claude Opus 4.6 agent Brier 0.130; second Opus run 0.130; mean of 4 runs (2 Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.4) 0.125, about 0.005 gain. About $0.55 per question per Opus run. Best forecaster in the related paper 0.011 better than one Opus agent.
limits: Blog (read via fetch summary), no CIs; the average mixes model families, so it confounds copies with diversity; no matched single stronger run; a separate post on the Claude effort parameter has no numbers.
agent_relevance: Gap 1/4/9: a recent measurement of about 0.005 gain for 4 mixed runs of frontier reasoning models, similar in size to Halawi's 0.003 and AIA's 0.004. The gain has not vanished as models improved.

source: Lu and Zhang (2026) The Corroboration Illusion, arXiv 2609.22246: clean performance and per-document median
finding: Retrieval raised the mean forecast and hurt Brier for small models. A system prompt stressing base rates and discounting speculative coverage halved the bias. Forecasting once per retrieved document and taking the median removed most of the optimism bias.
numbers: 500 ForecastBench questions, 17.4M-article crawl with date cutoff. Qwen2.5-7B Brier: no retrieval 0.159 (mean p 0.33); RAG 0.250 (mean p 0.49); RAG with calibrated base-rate prompt 0.184 (mean p 0.39); base-rate-only baseline 0.127; market price at freeze 0.074. Mean forecast 0.20 with none to 0.46 with 3-5 documents. Per-document median aggregation: Brier 0.250 to 0.222. Hermes-3-8B: no retrieval 0.192, RAG 0.226.
limits: Small open 7-8B models only; calibrated prompt also used higher relevance threshold and fewer docs (5 vs 10), so effects are bundled; retrieval still did not beat no-retrieval or the base-rate baseline.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: two cheap fixes with measured effect: a base-rate-first prompt (0.250 to 0.184) and one forecast per document with a median (0.250 to 0.222). Neither reached the base-rate-only 0.127, so for small models retrieval stayed net negative.

source: Lu and Zhang (2026) The Corroboration Illusion: poisoning and three defenses
finding: A fabricated article is treated as strong evidence regardless of publisher. Allow-lists, isolate-and-aggregate and perplexity filtering each have a cheap bypass. Stricter relevance filtering makes poison a bigger share of what survives.
numbers: Flip across 0.5: 1 article 56%; 5 articles 69-73%; 10 articles 89%. 5 injected articles: net shift +0.13 to +0.22; Brier 0.18 to 0.37. Allow-list: obscure publisher 14% flips, spoofed publisher 77%. Isolate-aggregate (median over per-document forecasts): k=1 flips 18% (noise floor 12-13%), k=5 flips 52% (YES), 40% (flip direction). Perplexity filter at 5% false positive removes 100% of default-generated poison, but at T=1.2 sampling detection falls to 31% and 67% still flip. Poison at 75% of kept documents gives +0.39.
limits: Injected in memory, not on the live web; 7-8B models; attacker is assumed to write many articles; larger models might be more sceptical (authors say unknown).
agent_relevance: Gap 5: no tested defense removes poison without losing genuine news. Median-over-documents helps only while poison is a minority; provenance needs signed feeds. For our agent: treat any single dramatic article as unverified, require independent corroboration across source types, and cap how far one document may move the forecast.

source: Hindcast (2026) Replaying Prediction Markets to Evaluate LLM Forecasters, arXiv 2607.14051
finding: With retrieval pinned to an immutable pre-cutoff Reddit archive (leak-free by construction), a retrieval agent still lowers Brier on eight of nine small open models. It helps where pre-event discussion carried facts and hurts where it carried hype.
numbers: 216 Polymarket markets, 25 monthly Reddit snapshots. Brier zero-shot to retrieval agent: Qwen3-4B .245 to .218; Qwen3-8B .234 to .179; Llama-3.1-8B .250 to .230; Gemma-3-4B .297 to .262; Gemma-3-27B .214 to .184; Ministral-8B .281 to .242; Llama-3.2-3B .375 to .292; one model (Qwen-7B R1-distill) did not improve overall. Best gain up to 23% (abstract). Topic net effect: Sports +16, Awards +12, Trading +7; Entertainment -31 (Billboard #1 questions, nearly all No), Other -10, Elections -7.
limits: Reddit only (20 subreddits); 83% of resolved markets are NO; small open models up to 27B; no frontier models; per-model run std shown in the paper but no formal tests.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: retrieval gain survives leak-free retrieval for small models, so the benefit is not only leakage. It is topic dependent and can reverse when the corpus holds speculation, which supports a guardrail: check evidence type before moving from the base rate.

source: Paleka, Sudhir, Alvarez, Bhat, et al. (2025) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters (ICLR 2025), arXiv 2412.18544
finding: Consistency scores correlate with Brier across forecaster models, but only for some checks, and part is just model strength. Building a forecaster that patches its answers toward consistency fixed the checked violations but did not improve real forecast accuracy.
numbers: Correlation with Brier (Table 2): Cond 0.92/0.87 (scraped, arbitrage/frequentist) and 0.71/0.69 (NewsAPI); CondCond 0.78/0.71 and 0.75/0.69; And 0.68/0.72 and 0.54/0.71; Negation 0.60/0.67 scraped but -0.36/-0.13 NewsAPI; Or 0.14/0.24 and -0.24/-0.31; ExpEvidence 0.20/0.77 and -0.11/0.06. MMLU error vs Brier is 0.38 and 0.55 for comparison. ArbitrageForecaster improves consistency on optimised checks but not held-out checks and does not improve forecasting performance.
limits: Correlations are across a handful of different forecaster models, not across runs of one model; nobody has tested consistency as a weight or filter among ensemble members.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: no evidence that consistency violations can pick or weight ensemble members. The earlier claim K14 (r up to 0.9) is across models and only for some checks. Keep it as a monitor, not a filter.

source: Temporal Leakage in Search-Engine Date-Filtered Web Retrieval (2026), arXiv 2602.00758
finding: Date-filtered Google and DuckDuckGo search leak post-cutoff content for most questions, and leaky evidence changes scores a lot. The study has no closed-book baseline, so it cannot say how much real retrieval gain remains.
numbers: 393 resolved Metaculus questions (389 usable). Major leakage for 71% of questions on Google and 81% on DuckDuckGo. gpt-oss-120b Brier 0.108 with leaky documents vs 0.242 where no post-cutoff info (73.5% of cases); full-leakage cases (2.6%) 0.129.
limits: One model, one question set, no no-search comparison reported.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: leaves the exact Halawi-with-leak-check number open. Combined with d09 and d18, leak-free retrieval is worth about 0.01 Brier for a strong agent and more for weak models, much less than the 0.108-vs-0.242 swing from leakage.

source: Search snippet only: news-augmented forecasting failure modes, arXiv 2511.18394 (via web search summary)
finding: Summary says news context helps in some domains and hurts in others, with failure modes of rumour overweighting, definition drift and recency bias.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; snippet-level only; do not cite for numbers.
agent_relevance: Consistent with d16 and d18 (news-based inflation and hype), but unverified.
